newsitem.title: JAPAN: Global accounting rule may revive Japan stocks.
newsitem.headline: Global accounting rule may revive Japan stocks.

text.p: Planned changes to Japan's accounting standards should make it easier to see the real value of listed companies, making some of them more attractive to stock investors, analysts say.

"Japanese firms indeed have a tremendous amount of latent profits off their balance sheets," said Yasuhiro Matsumoto, senior associate director of the financial advisory service at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.
The new accounting rules should also help change the belief that it is difficult to find out the financial condition of Japanese companies, Matsumoto said.

"Of course, some companies may suffer as a result, but it will surely widen the range of investors in the stock market, as the level of transparency in balance sheets will increase, and foreign investors, in particular, will be able to buy stocks more easily," he said.
Scared of being left behind in the global move towards international standards, Japan is working on a review of its domestic accounting methods.
The Ministry of Finance (MOF) plans to announce a draft of the changes by the end of this year, the first overall review in 20 years, market sources said.
Current accounting rules require corporations to disclose the financial statement of a subsidiary only if 50 percent of the unit's shares are owned by the parent firm.
Under the new standards, companies would have to disclose all of their group earnings if they are involved in the management of a subsidiary.
The Finance Ministry's draft is also likely to call for the introduction of mark-to-market accounting, the sources said.
Japanese companies partly use the rule now, and are likely to evaluate all of their assets based on the rule by the end of 1999/2000 financial year, they said.
Japanese firms' balance sheets are historically based on purchase prices. This means the older the company, the lower the value of its assets, compared with their current market value, analysts said.

"To overseas investors, it looks like Japanese companies are hiding their profits and not showing the real value of their assets," said Tamizo Kimura, chief strategist at Yamaichi Research Institute of Securities & Economics Inc.
Analysts said the hidden profits help Japanese companies absorb huge losses if they encounter a major crisis.

For instance, major Japanese trading house Sumitomo Corp announced that it would offset part of its massive $2.6 billion losses from a copper trading scandal through the sale of equity and real estate holdings.
Kimura said the introduction of the new standards, coupled with developments in government policies for land transactions, would help improve sentiment in the banking sector.
Japanese banks have suffered a great deal due to the slide in land prices after the bursting of the country's economic "bubble" of inflated prices in the early 1990s.
In Japan, loans are collateralised by real estate property.
Besides banks, many old firms, whose assets were valued at their purchase prices years ago, will be revalued, and their stock prices should go up, Kimura said.
